section_summary: This section completes an account of Japan’s cooperative newspaper-distribution system and contains Chugo Koito’s detailed survey of postwar newspaper production, newsroom organization, the Kyodo News Service, and Occupation-era journalism. It then reproduces a series of 1945 SCAP directives governing press freedom, censorship, radio, motion pictures, newsprint allocation, communications, and the suspension of particular news organizations and newspapers. The final pages begin an alphabetical biographical directory of leading figures in the Japanese press and broadcasting industries.

subfiles.title: Newspaper Distribution System
subfiles.about: Explains the history, operation, and likely reorganization of Japan's cooperative newspaper-distribution system.
subfiles.summary: Newspaper distribution from the prewar free-sales system through wartime control bodies to the postwar Newspaper Cooperative Distribution League, with its regional structure and functions; reorganization under the Economic Decentralization Law should preserve stable home delivery.

subfiles.title: Shop Talk of Newspaper Publishing in Japan
subfiles.about: Surveys the postwar Japanese press's editorial practices, manual typesetting, newsroom organization, news services, and adaptation to democratic journalism.
subfiles.summary: Koito contrasts prewar praise with postwar efforts at clearer reporting under the Occupation, explains laborious hand composition of Japanese characters, newspaper and Kyodo departments and Kyodo's reliance on foreign agencies, page organization, provincial editions, circulation features and GHQ press officials' influence.

subfiles.title: Freedom of Speech and Press
subfiles.from: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, signed Harold Fair
subfiles.to: Imperial Japanese Government, through Yokohama Liaison Office
subfiles.about: Sets initial Occupation rules for truthful reporting, public tranquility, military information, and radio news.
subfiles.summary: Memorandum calls for minimal limits on discussion while barring false reporting, destructive criticism, unreleased troop movements and order-disturbing rumors; radio is limited to Radio Tokyo news, music and entertainment, and SCAP may suspend offending publications or stations.

subfiles.title: Press Code for Japan
subfiles.from: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, signed Harold Fair
subfiles.to: Imperial Japanese Government, through Central Liaison Office, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Establishes ten rules requiring truthful, non-propagandistic newspaper reporting under the Occupation.
subfiles.summary: Press Code: strict factual accuracy and nothing disturbing public tranquility or fostering resentment toward the Allies; no editorializing in news, propaganda coloring, omitting pertinent facts or manipulative layout prominence.

subfiles.title: Radio Code for Japan
subfiles.from: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, signed Harold Fair
subfiles.to: Imperial Japanese Government, through Central Liaison Office, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Prescribes standards for Japanese news, entertainment, educational, and commercial radio programming.
subfiles.summary: Radio Code applies factuality, public-order and anti-propaganda rules to news and commentary and comparable rules to entertainment and information, barring themes disparaging Allied forces, with commercial scripts under the same policies.

subfiles.title: Disassociation of Press from Government
subfiles.from: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, signed Harold Fair
subfiles.to: Imperial Japanese Government, through Central Liaison Office, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Orders the Japanese government to remove official control and preferential monopolies from press and news services.
subfiles.summary: Directive: the government must remove barriers to news, end direct or indirect press control, give domestic and international agencies equal communications access, allow foreign wireless news, and temporarily keep the censored domestic distribution system until private alternatives emerge.

subfiles.title: Clarification of Censorship Directive
subfiles.from: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, signed Harold Fair
subfiles.to: Imperial Japanese Government, through Central Liaison Office, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Clarifies which Occupation announcements and local broadcasts count as officially released information.
subfiles.summary: SCAP says its and local headquarters' communications publish only after public-relations clearance; local radio may carry approved occupation, food and environmental news, other news stays with Radio Tokyo; this answers Japan's questions on the September 10 directive.

subfiles.title: Further Steps toward Freedom of Press and Speech
subfiles.from: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, signed Harold Fair
subfiles.to: Imperial Japanese Government, through Central Liaison Office, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Orders suspension and repeal of Japanese laws and practices restricting press, communications, and public expression.
subfiles.summary: Directive suspends peacetime and wartime restrictions on newspapers, communications, films, mail and expression except SCAP-approved censorship, bars punitive action, compulsory press organizations, bans and coercion of editorial policy, and requires repeal of listed laws with twice-monthly compliance reports.

subfiles.title: Suspension of the Domei News Agency
subfiles.from: Public Relations Office, General Headquarters, United States Army Forces, Pacific
subfiles.about: Announces the Supreme Commander's order completely suspending the Domei News Agency.
subfiles.summary: Press release: the Supreme Commander ordered the entire suspension of the Domei News Agency.

subfiles.title: Request for Information on Paper Industry
subfiles.from: R. C. Gramer, Chief, Economic and Scientific Section
subfiles.to: Mr. Ohta, Central Liaison Office, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Requests detailed production, inventory, control, and allocation information concerning Japanese newsprint and magazine paper.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum asks for current production figures, mill locations, production constraints, and estimates of output possible after those constraints are remedied. It also requests stock estimates and descriptions of manufacturing, distribution, and consumer-allocation controls, with a deadline of October 7.

subfiles.title: Elimination of Japanese Government Control of the Motion Picture Industry
subfiles.from: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, signed H. W. Allen
subfiles.to: Imperial Japanese Government, through Central Liaison Office, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Orders suspension and repeal of Japanese censorship and police-control laws affecting films, newsreels, and theatrical workers.
subfiles.summary: Directive extends press liberalization to films and newsreels, forbids punishing lawful expression, lists national and Tokyo laws to be voided or repealed for censorship and police supervision, allows safety and zoning rules temporarily, and aims at an autonomous industry committee and democratic films.

subfiles.title: Revision of Requirement for Printing Materials
subfiles.from: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, signed H. W. Allen
subfiles.to: Imperial Japanese Government, through Central Liaison Office, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reduces printing materials available to the Mainichi, Yomiuri, and Asahi for specified periodic newspaper editions.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum directs reductions in materials supplied to the three major newspaper companies for 215,000 single-sheet newspapers every third week. It specifies revised weekly quantities of newsprint, printing ink, wrapping, and tying materials and requires acknowledgment.

subfiles.title: Elimination of Newspaper Publishers' Associations Control over Distribution of Paper
subfiles.from: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, signed H. W. Allen
subfiles.to: Imperial Japanese Government, through Central Liaison Office, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transfers control of newsprint and book-paper rationing from publishers' associations to a government-created representative organization.
subfiles.summary: Japan must take paper distribution from the Japan Newspaper League and Publishers' Association, set separate newsprint and foreign-type paper sections including officials, large and small publishers and disinterested members, and disclose rationing policies, monthly allocations and rejected applicants.

subfiles.title: November 1945 Allotments of Foreign Paper and Newsprint
subfiles.from: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, signed H. W. Allen
subfiles.to: Imperial Japanese Government, through Central Liaison Office, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Keeps November paper and newsprint allotments at October levels pending creation of the new rationing organization.
subfiles.summary: Temporary rule: November 1945 allocations of foreign paper and newsprint stay identical to October's while Japan's paper-rationing organization is established.

subfiles.title: Control of Radio Communications
subfiles.from: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, signed H. W. Allen
subfiles.to: Imperial Japanese Government, through Central Liaison Office, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Requires advance registration of changes to Japanese radio circuits, broadcast stations, equipment, frequencies, and ownership.
subfiles.summary: Directive bars unregistered additions or changes to radio circuits and stations and requires English notice to SCAP's Civil Communications Section ten days ahead; silence isn't permanent approval, and SCAP may demand later modification.

subfiles.title: Suspension of Newspaper Ise Shimbun
subfiles.from: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, signed H. W. Allen
subfiles.to: Imperial Japanese Government, through Central Liaison Office, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Orders a two-day suspension of the daily newspaper Ise Shimbun.
subfiles.summary: Japan must suspend the Ise Shimbun from 0001 hours December 27 through 2400 hours December 28, 1945.

subfiles.title: Who's Who in the Japanese Press
subfiles.about: Provides alphabetical biographical entries for prominent Japanese newspaper, news-agency, and broadcasting figures.
subfiles.summary: The directory begins with Chotaro Abe and proceeds alphabetically through the opening of Tamon Maeda's entry. Entries identify current posts, birthplaces and dates, education, career histories, publications, foreign assignments, and residential addresses. The subjects include newspaper presidents, editors, business managers, correspondents, Kyodo and Jiji officials, NHK executives, former diplomats, politicians, and purged wartime press figures.
